name: Roman Catholic
blurb: A nuptial Mass or a marriage ceremony without Mass in a parish church, with the preparation course, certificates and family customs that come with it.

events.name: Blessing of an engaged couple
events.when: Around the engagement, 12 to 18 months before
events.description: A short blessing from the Book of Blessings, given by a priest or deacon at the end of Mass or at home with the two families. It is not a betrothal contract and carries no legal weight, but many parishes offer it and it is a natural moment to introduce the two families.

events.name: Marriage preparation
events.description: Required by the Church before the wedding. The format varies: a diocesan pre-Cana day, an Engaged Encounter weekend, a series of evenings with a sponsor couple, or in Ireland an Accord course. Most dioceses also ask you to complete a relationship inventory such as FOCCUS or Prepare/Enrich, which the facilitator scores and then discusses with you.

events.name: Serenata
events.description: An Italian custom, strongest in central and southern Italy. The groom arrives under the bride's window with musicians and friends and sings to her; she comes out and food and drink follow. Regional, not part of the liturgy.

events.name: Hen and stag celebrations
events.description: Called a bachelorette and bachelor party in the US, a despedida de soltera in the Philippines and much of Latin America, and a hen and stag in Ireland and Britain. Usually organised and paid for by the wedding party rather than the couple.

events.name: Civil ceremony or registration
events.when: Days or weeks before, or the same morning
events.description: Needed only in countries where a church wedding does not carry civil effect on its own. In France, Mexico and several other countries a civil ceremony at the town hall is separate and must come first. In Ireland, Italy, Spain, Poland, the UK and the US the church wedding is normally registered civilly at the same time, so no separate ceremony is needed. Ask the priest which applies where you are marrying.

events.name: Rehearsal and rehearsal dinner
events.when: The evening before, or a week or two before
events.description: The priest walks the wedding party, readers and musicians through the order of the liturgy. In Ireland the rehearsal is often held a week or two ahead rather than the night before. The rehearsal dinner is largely a US and Irish custom; in Italy, Poland and the Philippines it is less common. This is when you would normally hand over the civil licence or registration form and any offerings.
events.hosts: Traditionally the groom's family in the US

events.name: The wedding liturgy
events.description: Either the Order of Celebrating Matrimony within Mass, which runs roughly an hour to an hour and a quarter, or the Order without Mass, which runs around 30 to 45 minutes. In the Latin Church the couple themselves are the ministers of the sacrament; the priest or deacon receives their consent on behalf of the Church. Two witnesses are required and they do not have to be Catholic.
events.hosts: The couple, in the parish church

events.name: Photographs and receiving line
events.description: Posed family photographs are usually taken at the church door or inside once the liturgy has finished and the priest has agreed. Build in more time than you expect: large Catholic weddings often have four or five generations of both families to photograph, plus sponsors or padrinos.

events.name: Drinks reception
events.description: The gap between church and meal, usually an hour to two hours. In Ireland this is often the longest part of the day and includes tea, sandwiches and a bar. In Italy the aperitivo before the meal can itself be a substantial spread.

events.name: Wedding reception
events.description: The meal, speeches, cake and dancing. Length and shape vary widely: an Italian reception can run six or more hours with many courses and a midnight plate of pasta, a Polish reception runs to dawn, an Irish reception typically has an evening 'afters' guest list on top of the daytime one, and a Filipino reception often includes a formal programme with the principal sponsors introduced by name.
events.hosts: Traditionally the bride's family; now commonly shared or paid by the couple

events.name: Day-after gathering
events.description: Standard in Poland, where the poprawiny is a second full party for close family and friends. Common in Ireland as a relaxed lunch or barbecue for guests who travelled, and in Italy as a family lunch. Rarer in the US and the Philippines.

items.name: Church offering
items.note: The donation to the parish for use of the church, heating, lighting and administration. Canon law forbids charging for the sacrament itself, so this is framed as an offering rather than a price, and no couple should be turned away for being unable to pay. In practice most parishes publish a suggested amount, and it is often noticeably higher if neither of you is a registered parishioner. In Ireland it is normal for the offering to be larger when you marry outside your own parish.

items.name: Offering to the priest or deacon
items.note: A personal offering to the celebrant, given separately from the parish fee, usually in an envelope handed over at the rehearsal. There is rarely a stated figure. Take into account the preparation meetings and the rehearsal as well as the day itself. If a priest travels from another parish or diocese, cover his travel and accommodation too.

items.name: Altar servers and sacristan
items.note: A small thank-you envelope each for the servers, and for the sacristan who opens the church and sets up. Some parishes include this in the church fee; ask so you do not pay twice.

items.name: Marriage preparation course
items.note: Required before a Catholic wedding. Cost depends on format: a diocesan workshop day, an Engaged Encounter weekend with accommodation, sessions with a sponsor couple, or an Accord course in Ireland. There is usually a separate small fee for scoring the FOCCUS or Prepare/Enrich inventory. Online courses are widely available but many dioceses accept them only in special circumstances, so confirm before you book and pay.

items.name: Natural family planning session
items.note: Required in some dioceses and merely offered in others. Introductory sessions are often free; a full course with an instructor is not. Ask your parish whether it is required where you are marrying rather than assuming.

items.name: Certificates and document fees
items.note: Newly issued baptismal and confirmation certificates from the parishes where you received those sacraments, letters of freedom, and postage or courier costs. Small individually, but they add up when records sit in another country and need translating, and when a certificate has to be reissued because it fell outside the six-month window.

items.name: Diocesan permission or dispensation
items.note: Applies if one of you is not Catholic, if you want to marry outside a Catholic church, or if a previous marriage needs a declaration of nullity or a lack-of-form ruling. Diocesan tribunals do not generally charge for permissions, but nullity cases can carry an administrative fee and always carry a long lead time. Budget the time more than the money.

items.name: Civil licence or registration
items.note: Separate from anything the church charges. In the US, a county marriage licence, which usually expires 30 to 90 days after issue and in a few states carries a waiting period of three to six days. In Ireland, three months notice to the HSE registrar and the Marriage Registration Form. In England and Wales, notice at your local register office, plus a registrar's attendance fee if your church does not have an authorised person. In Italy, the pubblicazioni or a declaration at the town hall for non-residents.

items.name: Parish wedding coordinator
items.note: Many larger parishes have their own coordinator who runs the rehearsal, manages the church on the day and enforces the parish rules on flowers, photography and timings. Sometimes included in the church fee, sometimes charged separately, and occasionally mandatory even if you already have a wedding planner.

items.name: Church organist, cantor and musicians
items.note: Most parishes expect you to use their organist and cantor, or to get approval before bringing in outside musicians. A cantor matters more at a Catholic wedding than couples expect, because the responsorial psalm is meant to be sung and the congregation is meant to join in. Extra players such as a string quartet, trumpet or traditional Irish musicians are priced on top.

items.name: Church flowers
items.note: Altar arrangements and pew or aisle ends. Two things catch couples out. During Lent, floral decoration of the church is not permitted in most dioceses, and during Advent it should be restrained. During Christmas and Easter the church is already decorated and parishes usually ask you not to add to it or remove anything. If another wedding follows yours the same day, agreeing to share the cost is normal.

items.name: Flowers for Our Lady
items.note: A small bouquet the couple places at a statue or shrine of the Blessed Virgin Mary, often while the Ave Maria or a Marian hymn is sung. Devotional rather than required, and not part of the rite itself. Several dioceses ask that it be a genuine moment of prayer rather than a staged photograph, and that it happen after the Prayer after Communion rather than in the middle of the liturgy.

items.name: Arras, lazo, veil and candles
items.note: The physical items for the optional ritual elements: a cask of thirteen arras coins, a lazo or yugal cord, a ceremonial veil, and unity or sponsor candles. Central to Filipino, Mexican and other Hispanic weddings and a normal expense there; not used at all in most Irish, Polish or Italian weddings. In Latin American and Filipino practice the padrinos or sponsors traditionally buy these rather than the couple.

items.name: Reception venue hire
items.note: Hotel function room, parish hall, restaurant or marquee. Parish halls are often the cheapest option and sometimes come with conditions on alcohol and finish times. In Ireland and Britain hotels frequently set a minimum number of paying guests for a Saturday; in Italy the villa or agriturismo fee is often quoted separately from catering.

items.name: Wedding meal
items.note: Usually the single largest line. Expect a longer meal than at a secular wedding in Italy, where five or more courses is normal, and a substantial one in Poland, where hot food continues through the night. Check whether service charge, corkage and cake-cutting fees are included in the per-head price.

items.name: Bar and wine
items.note: Table wine, toast drink and whatever you cover at the bar. Polish receptions traditionally include vodka on the tables and a bread, salt and vodka welcome from the parents. If your reception is in a parish hall, check the alcohol policy before you plan anything.

items.name: Drinks reception and canapés
items.note: The gap between church and meal. In Ireland this stretch is long, because guests travel from the church and the hotel usually serves tea, sandwiches and a bar. In Italy the aperitivo can be an event in itself. Budget for it properly rather than treating it as a small extra.

items.name: Wedding cake
items.note: In Italy the cake is often a millefoglie or a tiered fruit-and-cream torta nuziale cut late in the evening. In Ireland and Britain fruit cake with a saved top tier is still common. In the Philippines and Latin America the cake is frequently sponsored by a named padrino or ninong rather than paid for by the couple.

items.name: Rehearsal dinner
items.note: Strongly established in the US, where the groom's family traditionally hosts and the guest list covers the wedding party, immediate family and out-of-town guests. Much smaller or absent in Italy, Poland and the Philippines, where the equivalent money tends to go into the reception itself.

items.name: Day-after gathering
items.note: The Polish poprawiny is a genuine second party with food, drink and music, and should be budgeted as one. The Irish day-after and the Italian family lunch are usually simpler. Turn this on only if your families expect it, and if they do, expect a real cost rather than a token one.

items.name: Wedding dress and alterations
items.note: Many parishes have no written dress code, but some do ask for shoulders covered in church, and a few cathedrals and shrine churches are stricter. If your dress is strapless and you would rather not be told on the morning, ask the parish directly and consider a bolero, wrap or mantilla for the liturgy.

items.name: Veil, shoes and accessories
items.note: A Spanish or Latin American bride may wear a lace mantilla rather than a tulle veil. In Poland the veil has a second life at midnight during the oczepiny, when it is removed and thrown, so factor that in if you were planning to keep it pristine.

items.name: Groom's outfit
items.note: Suit, morning dress or hire. At a Filipino wedding the groom and the male sponsors normally wear the barong tagalog, and buying one for each principal sponsor is a real cost that surprises couples marrying abroad.

items.name: Wedding party outfits
items.note: Bridesmaids, groomsmen and children. Who pays varies enormously by country and family. Catholic weddings often have a larger wedding party than average, particularly Filipino weddings with six to eight secondary sponsors on top of the usual attendants, so decide early who is covering what.

items.name: Hair and make-up
items.note: Trial plus the morning itself. If the church is some distance from where you are getting ready, add travel time for the stylist and be realistic about a ceremony that may start earlier than a secular wedding.

items.name: Wedding party hair and make-up
items.note: Bridesmaids and mothers. Priced per head and often the line that quietly doubles when the numbers settle.

items.name: Bouquets and buttonholes
items.note: Bridal bouquet, bridesmaids, buttonholes and corsages for parents. Add corsages for principal sponsors at a Filipino wedding and for padrinos and madrinas at a Latin American one, since they are formally recognised in the ceremony. If you plan to leave flowers for Our Lady, order a separate small posy rather than using your own bouquet.

items.name: Reception flowers and styling
items.note: Centrepieces, top table and any structural styling. If the church restricts what you can do there, this is where the flower budget tends to go instead.

items.name: Lighting and draping
items.note: Uplighting, festoons, dance floor. More relevant for parish halls and marquees than for hotels, which usually come dressed.

items.name: Photographer
items.note: Book someone who has shot in a Catholic church before. Most parishes ban flash during the liturgy, keep photographers out of the sanctuary, and restrict movement during the readings, the consent and Communion. A photographer who expects to roam freely will either be stopped on the day or will disrupt the Mass. Ask the parish for its written policy and send it on before the wedding.

items.name: Videographer
items.note: Same parish rules as for photographers, plus a common restriction on extra lighting and on placing a camera in the sanctuary. A fixed camera at the back with a microphone feed from the ambo often gets approved where a roaming operator does not, so ask early.

items.name: Band or main entertainment
items.note: In Ireland a live band for the main part of the night is close to standard. In Poland the band or wodzirej runs the whole reception, leads the oczepiny and keeps the floor going until dawn, so the booking is longer than a typical set. In Italy and the Philippines a smaller band or a hosted programme is more usual.

items.name: Late-night DJ
items.note: Usually takes over from the band. Confirm the venue's licensed finish time before booking extra hours.

items.name: Traditional musicians
items.note: A mariachi band at a Mexican wedding, an Irish trad group for the drinks reception, a rondalla at a Filipino reception, or a folk band in Poland. Almost always a reception cost rather than a church one, since parishes restrict church music to sacred repertoire.

items.name: Invitations and save the dates
items.note: Traditional Catholic wording names the parents as hosts and invites guests to the nuptial Mass rather than to a ceremony. If many guests are not Catholic, a short line about the timing of the church service and how to get to the reception saves a lot of questions.

items.name: Mass booklets
items.note: Longer and more expensive than a secular order of service, because they carry the readings, the responses, the hymns and usually a note explaining Communion for guests who are not Catholic. Most parishes want to check the text before it goes to print, so allow a fortnight between approval and printing.

items.name: On-the-day stationery
items.note: Table plan, place cards, menus, signage. If you have principal sponsors or padrinos, they are normally seated and named prominently, so allow for that in the plan.

items.name: Wedding cars
items.note: Bride and family to the church, couple to the reception. Ask about parking at the church, which is often the tightest constraint of the day, particularly at a city-centre parish on a Saturday.

items.name: Guest transport
items.note: A coach between church and reception is worth costing whenever the two are more than a short walk apart, which at a Catholic wedding they usually are, because the church is fixed by your parish and the reception is not.

items.name: Wedding rings
items.note: Both rings are blessed and exchanged during the liturgy, so bring them to the church and give them to the best man or an appointed bearer. In Ireland a Claddagh ring is sometimes used as a wedding band. In Latin American practice the rings are often bought by the padrinos de anillos.

items.name: Gifts for the wedding party and sponsors
items.note: Thank-you gifts for attendants, parents and readers. At Filipino and Latin American weddings this extends to the principal sponsors, padrinos and madrinas, which can be a long list. Where sponsors have paid for parts of the wedding, a considered gift matters more than usual.

items.name: Favours
items.note: In Italy the bomboniera with five sugared almonds is close to obligatory and is given to each family as they leave; the almonds are always an odd number. Elsewhere favours are optional and are one of the easiest lines to cut.

items.name: Wedding night accommodation
items.note: Your own room, and often rooms for parents or travelling family. Where the reception runs into the small hours, as in Poland and Ireland, on-site rooms for the wedding party are worth the cost.

items.name: Wedding insurance
items.note: Covers supplier failure, cancellation and damage. Some venues and marquee hire firms require public liability cover as a condition of booking, so check before you decline it.

timeline.task: Speak to your parish priest before you fix a date with anyone else
Ask which dates are unavailable: Good Friday and Holy Saturday are excluded outright, and Sundays, solemnities and the seasons of Advent, Lent and Easter carry restrictions
Book the church and get the date written into the parish diary
Decide with the priest whether it will be a nuptial Mass or the ceremony without Mass
Book the reception venue
Draft the guest list and agree with both families who is hosting and paying for what
Book the photographer and videographer, and ask the parish for its written photography policy
Book the band or main entertainment
Find out which parish holds each of your baptismal records, especially if you were baptised abroad
Enrol in the marriage preparation course, since diocesan places fill up well ahead
Start shopping for the dress, allowing for a long lead time plus alterations
If either of you is not Catholic, or was married before, ask the priest to begin the permission, dispensation or nullity process now
Send save the dates, particularly if guests are travelling internationally
Book the florist and confirm what the church allows in your wedding's liturgical season
Complete the marriage preparation course and keep the certificate
Complete the pre-nuptial enquiry with your priest, interviewed separately
Request letters of freedom from every parish where you have lived six months or more since turning eighteen
Choose your readings from the Lectionary options and agree them with the priest
Meet the parish music director and agree every piece, including processional and recessional
Request newly issued baptismal and confirmation certificates, dated within six months of the wedding
Order invitations
Send invitations
Confirm which optional ritual elements you want, such as the arras, lazo, veil or candles, and who will bring and place them
Give civil notice: the registrar in Ireland or the UK, the town hall in Italy, or check the licence window in your US state
Ask your readers, gift bearers and witnesses, and confirm your sponsors or padrinos
Attend the natural family planning session if your diocese requires it
Send the Mass booklet text to the priest for approval before printing
Send the parish photography and music rules to your suppliers in writing
Final meeting with the priest to walk through the order of the liturgy and hand over outstanding paperwork
Collect the civil marriage licence, watching the expiry window in the US and the one-month return deadline in Ireland
Rehearsal, and hand over the offerings and the civil paperwork
Go to confession before the wedding, as most couples are encouraged to do
If either of you was married before, or you are already married civilly, tell the priest at the first meeting — annulment and convalidation both take far longer than the rest of the planning

paperwork.item: Newly issued baptismal certificate, dated within six months of the wedding
paperwork.note: It must be a fresh copy rather than the one from your baptism day, because the parish adds notations for confirmation, ordination, religious vows and any previous marriage. Those notations are how the Church checks you are free to marry. Records held abroad can take months to obtain.

Canon 1065 asks Catholics who have not been confirmed to receive the sacrament before marriage where it can be done without serious inconvenience. Often the confirmation is noted on the baptismal certificate, which saves a second request.

paperwork.item: Pre-nuptial enquiry, also called the prenuptial questionnaire or investigation
paperwork.note: A formal interview with the priest, taken separately, under oath. It establishes that you are both free to marry, marrying freely, and intend a permanent, faithful marriage open to children.

paperwork.item: Letters or affidavits of freedom to marry
paperwork.note: Statements swearing you have never been married. In Ireland and Britain these usually come from the parish priest of each parish you have lived in for six months or more since turning eighteen. In the US they are more often sworn by your parents or by two people who have known you a long time.

paperwork.item: Certificate of completion of the marriage preparation course

paperwork.note: Needed when marrying a baptised non-Catholic Christian, under canon 1125. Requested by your priest from the bishop.
Needed when marrying someone who is not baptised, under canon 1086. A dispensation rather than a permission, so it takes a little longer.

paperwork.item: Promise concerning the baptism and Catholic upbringing of children
paperwork.note: A sincere promise to do all in your power to have children baptised and raised Catholic. The other party is not asked to promise anything, only to be informed of the promise you have made.

Needed if you want to marry somewhere other than a Catholic church, for example in your non-Catholic partner's own church before their minister. Without it the marriage is not valid in the eyes of the Church.

paperwork.item: Declaration of nullity, dissolution, or a death certificate
paperwork.note: This applies to a previous civil marriage too, not only a church one. Never set a date before the case is concluded; tribunals will not be rushed and a pending case is not a decision.

paperwork.item: Delegation for a visiting priest or deacon
paperwork.note: If a priest from outside the parish is to receive your consent, the parish priest must delegate him in writing. Without valid delegation the marriage is invalid, so confirm this in writing rather than assuming.

paperwork.item: Testimonial letters or nihil obstat between dioceses
paperwork.who: Both, if marrying outside your home diocese
paperwork.note: Your home parish sends your completed file to the wedding parish, usually via both chanceries. Allow several weeks.

No longer universally required. Canon 1067 leaves it to each bishops' conference, so it varies: the Diocese of Rome still posts them, Canada and Scotland have made them optional, and in Italy the civil pubblicazioni are a separate town hall requirement from which non-residents are usually exempt.

In the US, a county licence, typically valid 30 to 90 days with a waiting period of a few days in some states. In Ireland, three months notice to the HSE registrar and a Marriage Registration Form returned within one month of the wedding. In England and Wales, notice at your local register office, plus a registrar if your church has no authorised person. In Italy the church wedding carries civil effect under the concordat. In France and Mexico a separate civil ceremony must come first.

paperwork.item: Passport or photo identification and birth certificates

paperwork.note: A declaration of no impediment to marriage, obtained from your own country's consulate in Italy. Most Italian documents expire six months after issue, so time it carefully.

paperwork.item: Civil marriage certificate, if you are convalidating
paperwork.note: A couple already married civilly needs the certificate on the prenuptial file. The parish treats the wedding as a convalidation rather than a blessing, so allow the same lead time as a first marriage.

customs.name: The arras
customs.description: Thirteen coins, blessed and given by the groom to the bride and often passed back, symbolising everything they own being shared from now on. Usually explained as Christ and the twelve apostles. Standard in Spain, Latin America and the Philippines, and an approved option in the second edition of the Order of Celebrating Matrimony in the US. Almost never seen at Irish, Polish or Italian weddings.

customs.name: El lazo or yugal
customs.description: A cord, ribbon or oversized rosary laid over the couple's shoulders in a figure of eight, marking them as bound together. It goes on around the Lord's Prayer and nuptial blessing and is removed at the end. Mexican, wider Hispanic and Filipino practice; in Latin American weddings the padrinos de lazo place it, and in Filipino weddings two secondary sponsors do.

customs.name: The veil ceremony
customs.description: A veil pinned over the bride's head and the groom's shoulder, joining them under one cloth. Read as shelter, protection and shouldering burdens together. Filipino and Mexican practice, placed just before the nuptial blessing.

customs.name: The candle ceremony
customs.description: In Filipino weddings, sponsors light a candle on either side and the couple together light a third, for Christ as the light of the home. Note that this is not the same as the American unity candle, though they look alike.

customs.name: Principal and secondary sponsors
customs.description: In the Philippines the ninong and ninang are honoured guests and mentors, often several couples, named in the programme and standing with the couple. Six to eight secondary sponsors then handle the veil, cord, candle and coins. This is a formal role, not decoration.

customs.name: Padrinos and madrinas
customs.description: In Latin American practice, sponsoring couples who take on both a spiritual role and a specific expense: the lazo, the arras, the rings, the Bible and rosary, the kneeling cushions, the cake, the flowers. There may be a dozen or more pairs. It spreads the cost across the community rather than loading it on two families.

customs.name: The Bible and rosary
customs.description: Presented to the couple by their padrinos de biblia y rosario as a sign that the household will pray together. Latin American, occasionally Filipino.

customs.name: The unity candle
customs.description: Two candles lit from a central flame, or a single candle lit from two. Popular at American weddings and not part of the Catholic rite. Many dioceses discourage it inside the liturgy because it duplicates and distracts from the exchange of consent, and suggest placing it after the Prayer after Communion or moving it to the reception. Ask before printing it in the booklet.

customs.name: Flowers to Our Lady
customs.description: The couple lay flowers at a statue or shrine of the Blessed Virgin Mary and pray briefly, often while a Marian hymn is sung. Widespread and welcomed as devotion, but several dioceses ask that it be genuine prayer rather than a photograph, and that it come near the end of the liturgy.

customs.name: The mantilla
customs.description: A lace veil worn over a high comb rather than a tulle veil, sometimes black in older Spanish practice. Spanish and Latin American, and increasingly chosen elsewhere by brides who want their shoulders covered in church.

customs.name: Parental blessing before leaving for church
customs.description: Parents trace a cross on the couple's foreheads and bless them at home before they set out. Strong in Poland, where the couple traditionally kneel, and also found in Filipino and Latin American families.

customs.name: Bread, salt and vodka
customs.description: In Poland, the parents meet the couple at the reception door with bread, salt and a glass of vodka: bread so they never go hungry, salt for the hard times, vodka for the good ones. The glasses are then thrown and broken for luck.

customs.name: Oczepiny
customs.description: The Polish unveiling, around midnight. The bride's veil is removed to mark the passage into married life and thrown to the unmarried women, with the groom's tie thrown to the unmarried men. Usually run by the band leader and followed by games.

customs.name: Poprawiny
customs.description: A second, smaller Polish party the day after the wedding for close family and friends, with more food, more music and a finish in the afternoon or early evening. It is expected rather than a bonus.

customs.name: La serenata
customs.description: The Italian serenade under the bride's window the night before, with musicians and friends, followed by an impromptu party. Mainly central and southern Italy.

customs.name: Confetti and bomboniere
customs.description: Italian confetti are sugared almonds, never paper. They are given in odd numbers, five being usual, inside a bomboniera keepsake handed to each family as they leave. The tradition continues at anniversaries, silver at twenty-five years and gold at fifty.

customs.name: Rice at the church door
customs.description: Guests throw rice over the couple as they leave the church, for fertility and prosperity. Common in Italy and beyond, but check with the parish first: many churches now prohibit rice, confetti, petals and birdseed both inside and outside the building.

customs.name: Taglio della cravatta
customs.description: In parts of northern Italy the groom's tie is cut up by his friends and the pieces auctioned to guests, with the money going to the couple. Regional and light-hearted.

customs.name: La busta
customs.description: In Italy the usual wedding gift is cash in an envelope, given at the reception rather than sent in advance, and the amount is loosely expected to cover the cost of your seat. A gift list is far less common than in Ireland, Britain or the US.

customs.name: The money dance
customs.description: Guests pin banknotes to the couple, or pay for a short dance with them. Standard at Filipino receptions and common at Polish ones. Read as helping the new household start out, not as showing off.

customs.name: The Claddagh ring
customs.description: An Irish ring of two hands holding a crowned heart, for love, loyalty and friendship. Sometimes used as a wedding band, sometimes given as a gift, often handed down.

customs.name: The afters
customs.description: In Ireland, a second and larger evening guest list invited after the meal for the band, bar and finger food. It lets couples include a wide circle without a seated dinner for three hundred people.

customs.name: Confession before the wedding
customs.description: Many couples go to confession in the days before, sometimes with the wedding party. Not required for validity, but it is the usual pastoral advice and most parishes will arrange a time.

customs.name: Convalidation
customs.description: If you have already married civilly, the Church does not simply bless that marriage: it asks you to give consent again in a new act, because for Catholics the consent itself is the sacrament. A convalidation is a full wedding, usually small, and needs the same freedom-to-marry paperwork and preparation as any other. Couples are often surprised that a blessing of the civil marriage is a different thing and, in most dioceses, not the usual route.

gotchas: Talk to the parish before you book anything else. Most dioceses want at least six months notice and some ask for a full year, and popular churches book Saturdays a year or more ahead.

Marriage may not be celebrated at all on Good Friday or Holy Saturday. Lent and Advent are not closed seasons, but the Ritual Mass for Matrimony cannot be used on Sundays of Advent, Lent and Easter, on solemnities, or during Holy Week and the Easter octave. You can still marry on those days, but the prayers and readings come from the Mass of the day rather than from the marriage rite.
Lent brings a second restriction that surprises people more than the readings do: floral decoration of the church is not permitted in most dioceses during Lent, and should be restrained in Advent.

Saturday weddings that run into the evening can collide with the parish's vigil Mass, and Sunday weddings are refused by many parishes for the same reason. Ask about the time of day, not just the date.

Your baptismal certificate must be newly issued, usually within six months of the wedding, because the fresh copy carries the notations that prove you are free to marry. Requesting it too early is as much a problem as requesting it too late.

If either of you has been married before, including in a register office with no church involved, the case has to be resolved before a date can be set. Tribunal timelines are measured in months and sometimes years.
A priest from outside the parish must be formally delegated in writing by the parish priest. Get that confirmed rather than assumed; without it the marriage is invalid.

Catholic weddings normally take place in a parish church. A garden, hotel or beach ceremony requires a dispensation from canonical form, which is granted for serious reasons, and aesthetic preference is not one of them.

Church music is restricted to sacred music in most dioceses. Popular love songs are usually refused even as instrumentals, and some parishes also decline Wagner's Bridal Chorus and Mendelssohn's Wedding March because of their theatrical origins. Agree every piece with the parish music director before you promise a singer anything.

Photography rules are stricter than at a secular wedding: no flash during the liturgy, no entering the sanctuary, and limits on moving during the readings, the consent and Communion. Send your photographer the parish's written policy in advance.
Rice, confetti, petals and birdseed are prohibited at many churches, inside and out, and some parishes charge for cleaning if you go ahead anyway.

If one of you is not Catholic, the Church generally recommends the ceremony without Mass, because most of the congregation would not be able to receive Communion. Celebrating within Mass in that case needs the bishop's permission.
A minister from another church may be invited to read, preach or offer a blessing, but only the Catholic priest or deacon can receive your consent unless you have a dispensation from canonical form.
The unity candle and the sand ceremony are not part of the Catholic rite, and a number of dioceses ask that they be moved out of the liturgy or dropped. Confirm before you print the booklet.

The civil side is separate almost everywhere and has its own clock. A US licence can expire in as little as 30 days, Ireland needs three months notice to the registrar and the form returned within a month afterwards, and in France and Mexico the civil ceremony has to happen first.

Costs land in places couples do not plan for: the parish offering, a separate offering to the priest, the course fee, the inventory scoring fee, certificate and courier costs, and the parish coordinator. None is large on its own; together they are a real line.

If your families are from different Catholic cultures, agree early which customs are in. A Filipino family may expect eight named sponsors and a Polish family may expect a full second party the next day, and neither will read as optional to the people who expect it.

Irish.label: Irish

addItems.name: Handfasting ribbon
addItems.note: An Irish addition inside the Catholic rite, binding the couple's hands with a ribbon or cloth.

addCustoms.name: The Claddagh ring
addCustoms.description: Often used as the wedding ring or given alongside it.

addCustoms.name: Magic hankie
addCustoms.description: A lace handkerchief carried by the bride, later made into a christening bonnet.

addGotchas: In Ireland you must give three months' notice to the HSE registrar as well as completing the church paperwork, and the two run on separate clocks.

Polish.label: Polish

addEvents.name: The parents' blessing
addEvents.description: Both sets of parents bless the couple at home before they leave for the church. Quiet, brief and often the moment parents remember.

addEvents.name: Oczepiny
addEvents.description: The unveiling at midnight, followed by games and the passing of the veil to the next unmarried woman.

addEvents.name: Poprawiny
addEvents.description: The second day of the wedding, held for the same guests, with more food and less formality.

addItems.name: Bread and salt greeting
addItems.note: The parents greet the couple with bread, salt and vodka at the reception door.

addItems.name: Poprawiny catering
addItems.note: A second day of feeding the same guests. Polish weddings are routinely two days, and budgets that assume one are half right.

addTimeline.task: Decide whether you are having poprawiny, because it doubles the catering and the accommodation

addGotchas: A Polish wedding is commonly two days. Guests expect the poprawiny and will have booked accommodation accordingly.
Vodka is served at the table by the bottle rather than from a bar. Budget accordingly and tell a non-Polish venue what is coming.

Italian.label: Italian

addCustoms.name: La busta
addCustoms.description: Guests give money in envelopes at the reception rather than gifts from a list.

addCustoms.name: Confetti and bomboniere
addCustoms.description: Sugared almonds in odd numbers, presented in favours given to every guest.

addGotchas: Italian receptions run long and food-led — five or more courses is normal, and a three-hour venue hire will not work.

Filipino.label: Filipino

addItems.name: Cord, veil and arras
addItems.note: The veil, cord and thirteen coins, with sponsors appointed to place each. Central to a Filipino Catholic wedding.

addCustoms.name: Ninong and ninang
addCustoms.description: Principal sponsors, often many of them, who are named in the invitation and take a real role in the ceremony and its costs.

addCustoms.name: The money dance
addCustoms.description: Guests pin notes to the couple during a dedicated dance.

addGotchas: Filipino weddings can have a dozen or more principal sponsors, each named and each with a role. Agree the list early — it affects the seating, the programme and the invitations.

Latin American.label: Latin American

addItems.name: Las arras and el lazo
addItems.note: Thirteen coins and the lazo cord placed by padrinos during the mass.

addCustoms.name: Padrinos
addCustoms.description: Sponsor couples who fund specific elements — the cake, the flowers, the lazo — and are honoured in the programme.

addCustoms.name: La hora loca
addCustoms.description: The 'crazy hour' late in the reception: masks, props, horns and a change of tempo.

addGotchas: Padrinos traditionally fund named elements. Agreeing who sponsors what early avoids two families both buying the cake, or neither.

Other.label: Other
addGotchas: Diocesan requirements for paperwork and preparation courses vary more than couples expect, even between neighbouring dioceses.
